strengths: The idea of converting camera poses into pixel-wise embeddings is novel, which allow the video generation model to effectively understand the camera motion.
This paper studies three common ways of incorporating camera pose embedding into a DiT model, which could be useful for future work.
To the best of my knowledge, this is the first work that tackles camera-motion-controlled video generation with open-source DiT (i.e. opensora).
The idea of sparsely sampling motion fields before inputting them into the VAE encoder is new.

They demonstrate that adaptive normalization for conditioning camera motions is the effective strategy for camera-conditioned video generation for the first time, which is consistent with the results demonstrated in trajectory-controlled generation (e.g. Tora).
They quantitatively demonstrate that the generated videos have better motion and visual quality for 72-frame generation.
This paper train a VAE model to temporally downsample the Plücker embeddings, easing the conflict of different temporal length between Plücker embedding and the latent features.
The visualization results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on some simple camera trajectories, like paning and zooming.
The authors add the camera pose in the video generation, which is an interesting point.
weaknesses: The proposed sparse motion encoding module seems almost identical to the standard pixel-wise Plucker embedding. Compared with Eq. (3), the only difference in Eq. (4) is the embedding computation are performed on a set of sparse locations controlled by $s_x$ and $s_y$. It is not clear how the camera "motion" is encoded. Does the proposed approach convert the pixel-wise motion vectors shown in Fig. 4 into embeddings?
A lot of definitions are not clear and math symbols are not used rigorously in the presentation, making the paper hard to follow and understand.
The Sparse Motion Encoding Module and Temporal Attention Injection Module are not shown in Fig. 1 at all.
In line #179 on page 4, how is $RT$ defined? Is it matrix multiplication similar to $RK^{-1}$?
In line #195 on page 4, it says $F_s\in \mathbb{R}^{L\times M\times N}$? According to the definition in Eq.(4), the channel dimension shouldn't be 1?
In Fig. 2, $c_p$, $c_s$, and $c_l$ are not defined in the main text. And the shape of $c_l$ is not clearly explained either.
In Fig. 3, what are $s$, $p$, and $p_m$?
The first two items of the claim contributions of the paper are essentially identical. Both of them are about incorporating camera poses into a DiT model.

Only visual results of simple camera motion (zoom in, zoom out, and roundabout) are shown in the paper. No supplementary results are available. It is therefore hard to gauge the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
The idea of using Plucker coordinates has already been introduced (e.g., VD3D).
The use of a VAE encoder and adaptive normalization has already been introduced by Tora.

The main technical contribution is introducing a sparsely sampled motion field, but the authors fail to provide detailed results (e.g., visual results, more ablation study in Table 2, what about x1?) nor detailed motivation.
Choosing the downsample factor seems heuristic with no intuitive justification.
The authors should provide more ablation studies and technical motivations for applying sparsely sampled motion fields.
Although the model is trained on a 16-frame dataset, the model performs worse than other baselines for 16-frame generation.
The motivation for training only on 16-frame videos is unclear, given the model is tasked to generate longer-frame videos during the experiments.
The authors did not provide sufficient qualitative results or user study, where the superiority of their method is not convincing.
The paper lacks implementation details; for instance, it is not clear how adaptive normalization and cross-attention are performed exactly.
Figure 3 seems inaccurate because the injection happens between two temporal attention layers, where the temporal attention layer should exist in only one of these locations.
The motivation of Sparse Motion Encoding Module is not well presented; unclear why the VAE model is used to compress the Plücker embedding.
It is unclear what the decoder is used for in the VAE.
The reason for sparsely sampling some Plücker motion vectors is not justified.
VAE model will not bring much extra computation, and can be reused once encoded.
The manuscript contains typos (e.g., "MegVit-v2") and inconsistencies (OpenSora vs Open-Sora).
Some details are missing, such as the input of the Sparse Motion Encoding Module.
Rows 2 and 4 in Figure 4 do not provide much information.
The experiments is not very convincing. See Question part.

Many details are missing in Fig 2. I do not find any explanations of what does frame pose mean and how to get the frame pose. How to convert frame pose to camera pose is also very unclear. It would be helpful to provide a step-by-step description of how to extract and process the pose information from the dataset, including definitions of frame pose and camera pose, and the conversion process between them.

The method is only evaluated on a single dataset, which is not sufficient to verify the effectiveness of the method. For example, authors can test on videos from WebVid and HD-VILA following MotionCtrl [1] paper.
